newsitem.title: USA: U.S. mulls call for ban on tuna from three nations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mulls call for ban on tuna from three nations.

text.p: The United States next week might call for an international ban on imports of tuna from Panama, Honduras and Belize to pressure those governments to back tuna protection efforts, a U.S. official said on Friday.

The International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tuna (ICCAT), which is due to meet in San Sebastian, Spain on Nov. 22-29, warned the three countries, which are not members of the commission, last year that fishing of bluefin tuna by their ships was undermining conservation.
"This year we're considering final steps to authorise trade measures," said Will Martin, ICCAT's U.S. commissioner.

The move is intended to spur the many countries outside the commission to join it or cooperate with it to save the bluefin tuna, which has been depleted in the Atlantic by about 87 percent over the last 20 years. About 43,000 tons of tuna are caught annually worldwide.
Any tuna trade ban would be most heavily felt in Japan, which consumes up to 70 percent of the world's catch, according to the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF).
A Japanese official in Washington said Tokyo had yet to decide whether it would back international sanctions although it passed a law in June clearing the way for a ban.

Japan imported a total of 674 metric tons of bluefin tuna from Belize, Panama, and Honduras 1994. Tokyo's biggest concern is that restrictions might run afoul of the World Trade Organisation, Shingo Ota, First Secretary at the Japanese Embassy, said.

Washington believed a multilateral ban would be in line with WTO rules. The United States plans to focus on compliance with tuna and swordfish fishing allocations at the conference, including a call for 25 percent quota penalties for flouting of quotas.

The commission should clamp down on fishing of young tuna in Europe, which is blocking recovery of the species, Martin said. The United States also plans to call for a 2,000 metric ton reduction to 12,000 tons in North Atlantic swordfish fishing quotas but wants to maintain current quotas for tuna, a move which Martin said was more controversial.
Scientists recommended the U.S. bluefish tuna catch should be cut from more than 1,000 tons to 250 tons a year to rebuild the population over the next 20 years.
"That's viewed by the U.S. government as politically impossible," said Michael Sutton of WWF, pointing to heavy pressure from New England states on the Clinton administration to increase tuna quotas.

Fishermen claim they have been seeing more fish and have been filling quotas in record time, so the administration wants to gather more scientific evidence on the stocks over the next two years, Martin said.
